extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy, and critical reasoning; anyone learning to detect fallacies in argument
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and evaluating arguments by spotting ambiguous terms, question-begging, composition/division errors, and related fallacies. Emphasizes clarifying senses of words and exposing disguised circularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish persuasive influence from coercive influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase “influence of property” is ambiguous between influence arising from respect/gratitude and influence arising from fear or coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political arguments about influence, clarify whether the influence is persuasive (acting through conscience, beneficial) or coercive (compelling action against moral convictions, to be restrained). Confounding the two produces a standing fallacy of ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify senses of 'Theory' (proper vs vulgar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory in the proper acceptation means the completed result of philosophical induction (the explanation of practice); in the vulgar sense it means any mere fiction of the imagination about how something might possibly have been produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissing legitimate generalizations by attacking the vulgar sense. Ensure 'theory' is used consistently—if intended as generalization from evidence, treat it as a principle guiding practice rather than mere speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve collective-term ambiguity (e.g., 'The Church')
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective nouns like “The Church” can mean only the clergy or the whole body of believers (or communicants); this ambiguity affects claims such as inviolability of church property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify referents of collective terms. Do not assume managing members (e.g., clergy) are the actual owners; recognize usufruct/life-interest distinctions when evaluating property or institutional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent meanings across syllogistic premises (e.g., 'laudabile')
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Stoic example, the word _laudabile_ is used in the minor premise as anything admired (beauty, fortune) but in the major as exclusively moral qualities, producing a fallacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that key terms retain the same sense in all premises and the conclusion. A shift in meaning between premises yields invalid inferences even if the verbal form appears correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shifting pronoun/reference (ambiguity of 'I')
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes' argument equivocates with the pronoun _I_, sometimes meaning will, sometimes laws of my nature, producing an invalid conclusion about the origin of conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing arguments that use first-person or indexical terms, make the intended referent explicit (will, dispositions, laws of nature, actions) and check that it does not change across steps of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disambiguate psychological terms in free-will debates
rubrics_metrics.description: In free-will discussions words like 'I' (volitions vs actions vs mental dispositions) and 'necessity' (Certainty vs Compulsion; cannot be prevented vs will not) are often shifted or left unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precisely define whether 'necessity' denotes logical certainty, causal inevitability, or high probability. Distinguish internal mental conditions as caused by antecedents rather than assumed spontaneous, uncaused volitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish identity from similarity ('same' specie vs numero)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word _same_ is used both for exact numerical identity and for high similarity; confusing these leads to metaphysical errors (e.g., Plato's theory of Ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When 'same' is used, ask whether the claim is about one identical object existing across contexts (sameness numero) or about objects sharing characteristics (sameness specie). Beware inferences that require numerical identity when only similarity is supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate persistence of ideas with identity of an idea over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Berkeley's argument assumes that having the 'same idea' on different days implies the identical individual idea persisted, instead of merely similar ideas recurring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify temporal identity claims: 'the same thought' typically means same kind/similar thought, not the same numerically identical mental token. Avoid inferring a permanent bearer (e.g., a Universal Mind) from this confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify which measurable effect a physical term denotes (e.g., 'force')
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes like vis viva arose because 'force' was associated with different measurable effects (one effect ∝ velocity, another ∝ velocity^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scientific reasoning, define whether a term is intended to refer to momentum, vis viva, or another measure. If multiple relevant measures exist, acknowledge them rather than treating the term as a single unequivocal property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate infinite divisibility from infinite magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Achilles and the Tortoise puzzle confuses 'forever' in conclusion (any length of time) with 'ever' in premises (any number of subdivisions); unlimited subdivision does not imply unlimited total duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with infinities, be explicit whether you mean infinite divisibility (arbitrarily many subdivisions within a finite interval) or an infinite extent/duration. Avoid transferring quantification over subdivisions to quantification over total magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disambiguate 'right' (duties owed by others vs absence of duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'right' can mean a right that others are morally bound not to interfere, or merely the absence of a duty on oneself; it is often conflated with a right to enforce or punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish (a) rights grounded in duties owed by others, (b) permissive absence of duty on the actor, and (c) entitlement to enforce/punish. Evaluate claims about rights by specifying which sense is intended and weighing further practical considerations before inferring enforcement rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect Fallacy of Composition and Division (collective vs distributive shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy occurs when a term is collective in the premises and distributive in the conclusion (or vice versa), e.g., inferring that because each member could be replaced, the whole class is dispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether predicates applied to individual members are being illegitimately transferred to the whole, or properties of the whole are being ascribed to each member. Watch for hidden shifts of collective/distributive meaning in middle terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Petitio Principii / Begging the Question (including circular reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: A premise either appears to be the same as the conclusion, is proved from the conclusion, or can only be proved by the conclusion; reasoning in a circle is a stronger form where propositions are proved reciprocally from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose circularity by requesting independent proof of premises. Recognize disguised forms where premises presuppose the conclusion through restatement, abstract terms, or appeals to authority/traditional belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose disguises of question-begging (abstract/concrete restatement, essence claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common disguises include expressing the same proposition in abstract terms to make it seem different, invoking 'nature' or 'essence' claims that assume what they assert, or adopting 'question-begging appellatives' (loaded names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate abstract statements into concrete claims and test whether they really differ from the conclusion. Challenge appeals to 'nature' or 'essence' and ask for independent justification of such premises rather than taking them as self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using loaded or value-laden labels as premises ('question-begging appellatives')
rubrics_metrics.description: Words with laudatory or vituperative connotations (e.g., 'Innovation') can beg the question by smuggling an evaluative judgment into a premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace emotive labels with neutral descriptions of the proposition's features. Do not accept pejorative or laudatory terminology as proof of the claim they imply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of mistaking mutual coherence for independent truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of propositions that hang together coherently may be mistaken for being independently true; thinkers may accept mutually supporting premises that lack an external ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for independent points of support or contact with facts; mutual consistency alone is insufficient to establish truth. Challenge the system to provide a non-circular foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require proof even for premises that seem more obvious than the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that assume premises appearing more evident than their conclusions can still be petitio principii (e.g., assumption of impossibility of minimum thickness in infinite divisibility arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand justification for premises, regardless of intuitive plausibility. Identify whether an apparently obvious premise covertly assumes the conclusion or relies on the inability of imagination as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for paronymous/terminological confusions (e.g., cupiditas/cupidus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using related or derived words with different connotations (paronymous terms) can subtly alter meaning and beg the question, as when morally laden forms are substituted for neutral descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the etymology and connotation of key terms used in an argument. Check that derivations or adjectival forms are not being used to smuggle evaluative content into premises.
